title: Don't feel like working out?
description:
Here's what I do on "slow days" where I don't feel like doing a workout.

My rule of thumb: Do at least 5-10 minutes of the workout UNLESS I'm so exhausted I think it'll make me sick or injured.

However, a more important question I think we should start asking ourselves is WHY we have these "slow days."

If you routinely have long periods where you feel tired, you may want to look into some causes.

How is your diet? Is it balanced? Are there things you can change to get your required nutrients?

Are you getting enough sleep? 7-8 hours at least for the vast majority of people. If you are, how is your sleep quality?

While some may point to mental health issues - and they're certainly a valid cause - our lifestyle may be a contributing cause to that as well.

Everyone should look into optimizing their lifestyle a bit. There's no downside to it. 

Sometimes everything is fine, but our work is boring. If you've been stuck on the same routine for a while, try changing it up! What have you wanted to learn? Anything from backflips to tennis can be explored.

Just some thoughts! Hope that helps!

Regular exercise is crucial for maintaining good physical health, especially as women approach their 40s. One of the most significant benefits of exercise is a reduced risk of chronic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and certain types of cancer. These conditions can be especially prevalent as women age and are more prone to hormonal changes and lifestyle factors that contribute to disease. However, regular exercise has been shown to lower the risk of these conditions by improving blood sugar control, lowering blood pressure, and reducing inflammation.

In addition to reducing the risk of chronic diseases, exercise can improve cardiovascular health, which is essential for maintaining overall well-being. Exercise can strengthen the heart and blood vessels, reduce blood pressure, and improve cholesterol levels, all of which contribute to a healthy cardiovascular system. Improved cardiovascular health can also lead to increased endurance, making it easier for women to perform everyday activities without getting tired quickly.

Another physical benefit of getting fit at 40 is the improvement of muscle strength and bone density. As women age, they are more likely to experience a decline in muscle mass and bone density, which can lead to decreased strength and an increased risk of falls and fractures. However, regular exercise can help prevent or slow down this decline by stimulating muscle growth and strengthening bones.

Mental Benefits:
In addition to the physical benefits, getting fit at 40 can also have a significant impact on mental health. Exercise has been shown to reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, improve overall mood, and increase cognitive function. These benefits can be particularly important for women as they navigate the challenges of midlife, such as changes in hormonal balance and stressors related to work and family.

Research has shown that exercise can be as effective as medication for treating mild to moderate depression and anxiety. This is because exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters and can improve overall feelings of well-being. Additionally, exercise can be a way for women to reduce stress and improve their ability to manage stress in their daily lives.

Finally, exercise has been shown to have a positive impact on cognitive function, including memory, attention, and decision-making. This is important for women as they age, as cognitive decline can be a concern. Exercise can help maintain cognitive function and even improve it in some cases.

-Why consistency beats perfection every time

Extreme ownership

Jocko Willink is a retired U.S. Navy SEAL officer who served for over 20 years and commanded one of the most highly decorated special operations units during the Iraq War. Those battlefield lessons became the foundation of his life philosophy: if something in your life isn’t working, the responsibility is yours to fix.

After retiring from the military, Jocko became a bestselling author, leadership consultant, and host of the Jocko Podcast, where he teaches people how to apply military-grade discipline to everyday life. His message is simple but demanding: discipline equals freedom. Through structure, consistency, and personal accountability, anyone can build strength, confidence, and control over their life - regardless of their past, circumstances, or emotions.

title: How to Develop an Abundance Mindset | Jim Rohn Motivation
description:
Abundance is not luck 🍀 

It’s a way of operating.

This video breaks down what an abundance mindset actually is—and what it isn’t. Opportunity, wealth, and growth aren’t reserved for a select few. They expand in direct proportion to how you think, decide, and act. Scarcity isn’t a lack of resources. It’s a pattern of hesitation, fear, and narrow expectations.

🔑 Abundance begins with identity.

In this video, you’ll learn:
➖The real difference between scarcity and abundance thinking
➖How subconscious beliefs quietly shape outcomes
➖Why gratitude stabilizes confidence and momentum
➖How decisive action creates opportunity
➖How to align daily habits with growth and prosperity

Success isn’t something you chase. It responds to clarity, confidence, and consistency. When limiting beliefs are removed and actions rise to higher standards, opportunities become visible—and usable.

This video is for anyone tired of playing small, second-guessing decisions, or feeling boxed in by fear and self-doubt. Abundance grows when you stop waiting to deserve progress and start operating as someone who expects it.

Small shifts in thinking.
Clearer decisions.
Stronger follow-through.

That’s how abundance compounds.

This transcript and video were written & produced by Dus Rawling, inspired by the ideas and philosophies of Jim Rohn.

Regular exercise is crucial for maintaining good physical health, especially as women approach their 40s. One of the most significant benefits of exercise is a reduced risk of chronic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and certain types of cancer. These conditions can be especially prevalent as women age and are more prone to hormonal changes and lifestyle factors that contribute to disease. However, regular exercise has been shown to lower the risk of these conditions by improving blood sugar control, lowering blood pressure, and reducing inflammation.

In addition to reducing the risk of chronic diseases, exercise can improve cardiovascular health, which is essential for maintaining overall well-being. Exercise can strengthen the heart and blood vessels, reduce blood pressure, and improve cholesterol levels, all of which contribute to a healthy cardiovascular system. Improved cardiovascular health can also lead to increased endurance, making it easier for women to perform everyday activities without getting tired quickly.

Another physical benefit of getting fit at 40 is the improvement of muscle strength and bone density. As women age, they are more likely to experience a decline in muscle mass and bone density, which can lead to decreased strength and an increased risk of falls and fractures. However, regular exercise can help prevent or slow down this decline by stimulating muscle growth and strengthening bones.

Mental Benefits:
In addition to the physical benefits, getting fit at 40 can also have a significant impact on mental health. Exercise has been shown to reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, improve overall mood, and increase cognitive function. These benefits can be particularly important for women as they navigate the challenges of midlife, such as changes in hormonal balance and stressors related to work and family.

Research has shown that exercise can be as effective as medication for treating mild to moderate depression and anxiety. This is because exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters and can improve overall feelings of well-being. Additionally, exercise can be a way for women to reduce stress and improve their ability to manage stress in their daily lives.

Finally, exercise has been shown to have a positive impact on cognitive function, including memory, attention, and decision-making. This is important for women as they age, as cognitive decline can be a concern. Exercise can help maintain cognitive function and even improve it in some cases.

This isn’t motivation for a moment.

Listen carefully.

title: David Goggins is INSANE!
description:
David Goggins is widely regarded as one of the most inspirational figures in the world of personal development, endurance athletics, and mental toughness. His life story is a powerful example of resilience, determination, and the ability to completely transform oneself despite extreme adversity. He is a retired Navy SEAL, an ultra-endurance athlete, a former Air Force Tactical Air Control Party member, and a motivational speaker who has built a reputation for pushing the limits of human performance. What sets him apart is not simply his accomplishments, but the journey of hardship and transformation that forged his mindset and philosophy.

Goggins was born in 1975 in Buffalo, New York, into a difficult and traumatic childhood. His father was abusive, and the environment in which he was raised was filled with violence and instability. As a young boy, Goggins struggled academically, battled racism, and endured a household environment that was mentally and physically damaging. He also suffered from a learning disability, which made his time in school even more challenging. His early years gave him a sense of fear, insecurity, and lack of self-worth that stayed with him well into his young adulthood. At one point, he was overweight, unmotivated, and living a life that he himself described as unfulfilled and purposeless.

The turning point in his life came when he made the decision to join the United States military. At first, he joined the Air Force and served as part of the Tactical Air Control Party, but later he pursued the much more difficult path of becoming a Navy SEAL. His journey toward earning the SEAL trident was one of the most grueling aspects of his life. He failed to qualify multiple times due to injuries and setbacks, but his determination and refusal to quit ultimately carried him through. He went through the infamous Basic Underwater Demolition SEAL training, better known as BUD/S, three times before graduating. This period of his life became the foundation of the mental toughness principles he would later teach to millions.

As a Navy SEAL, Goggins served in combat zones and built his reputation as someone who embraced suffering and hardship as opportunities to grow. However, his challenges did not stop after his military career. He went on to pursue ultra-endurance athletics, which includes ultramarathons, long-distance cycling, and other extreme events that test physical and mental capacity. Despite being diagnosed with a heart condition early in his endurance career, he went on to complete some of the most brutal races in the world, including the Badwater 135 ultramarathon across Death Valley, Ironman triathlons, and countless other endurance challenges. He frequently competed with broken bones, torn muscles, or other injuries, but continued anyway, motivated by his mindset of never giving up.

What makes Goggins unique is not only his ability to endure extreme conditions but also his philosophy about suffering and personal growth. He developed the concept of the “cookie jar,” which is the practice of drawing strength from past victories and hardships whenever facing new challenges. He also emphasizes the “forty percent rule,” which suggests that when the human mind believes it has reached its limit, it is often only operating at about forty percent of its true capacity. Through discipline, grit, and self-mastery, he believes anyone can unlock hidden reserves of strength and resilience.

Goggins became widely known outside of the military and endurance community through his bestselling memoir “Can’t Hurt Me.” The book details his life story, his philosophy of accountability, and his approach to overcoming mental barriers. It resonated with millions around the world who were inspired by his honesty, rawness, and refusal to sugarcoat the realities of hardship. In the book, he introduced concepts like the accountability mirror, which involves confronting oneself with brutal honesty in order to make real change.

Beyond the book, Goggins has become a highly sought-after motivational speaker. He has spoken to Fortune 500 companies, sports teams, and individuals across the globe, sharing his philosophy of discipline, suffering, and resilience. His message often revolves around the idea that growth comes from discomfort and that most people live far below their potential because they avoid pain and challenges. Instead of seeking comfort, Goggins teaches that embracing hardship can forge an indomitable spirit and lead to extraordinary achievements.

Regular exercise is crucial for maintaining good physical health, especially as women approach their 40s. One of the most significant benefits of exercise is a reduced risk of chronic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and certain types of cancer. These conditions can be especially prevalent as women age and are more prone to hormonal changes and lifestyle factors that contribute to disease. However, regular exercise has been shown to lower the risk of these conditions by improving blood sugar control, lowering blood pressure, and reducing inflammation.

In addition to reducing the risk of chronic diseases, exercise can improve cardiovascular health, which is essential for maintaining overall well-being. Exercise can strengthen the heart and blood vessels, reduce blood pressure, and improve cholesterol levels, all of which contribute to a healthy cardiovascular system. Improved cardiovascular health can also lead to increased endurance, making it easier for women to perform everyday activities without getting tired quickly.

Another physical benefit of getting fit at 40 is the improvement of muscle strength and bone density. As women age, they are more likely to experience a decline in muscle mass and bone density, which can lead to decreased strength and an increased risk of falls and fractures. However, regular exercise can help prevent or slow down this decline by stimulating muscle growth and strengthening bones.

Mental Benefits:
In addition to the physical benefits, getting fit at 40 can also have a significant impact on mental health. Exercise has been shown to reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, improve overall mood, and increase cognitive function. These benefits can be particularly important for women as they navigate the challenges of midlife, such as changes in hormonal balance and stressors related to work and family.

Research has shown that exercise can be as effective as medication for treating mild to moderate depression and anxiety. This is because exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters and can improve overall feelings of well-being. Additionally, exercise can be a way for women to reduce stress and improve their ability to manage stress in their daily lives.

Finally, exercise has been shown to have a positive impact on cognitive function, including memory, attention, and decision-making. This is important for women as they age, as cognitive decline can be a concern. Exercise can help maintain cognitive function and even improve it in some cases.

title: Growth Mindset vs Fixed Mindset | Vusi Thembekwayo
description:
Vusi Thembekwayo talking about growth mindset.

Embracing the Growth Mindset

In the vast tapestry of life, we hold the threads of endless possibilities. It’s not just about where we stand today, but how far we can stretch our wings, expand our horizons, and evolve into the best versions of ourselves. Welcome to the realm of the growth mindset, a transformative perspective that fuels our journey of self-discovery, resilience, and achievement.

Imagine a mindset that sees challenges as opportunities, setbacks as stepping stones, and failures as invaluable lessons. A growth mindset embraces the belief that our abilities and intelligence are not fixed but can be nurtured, developed, and honed with effort, perseverance, and an unwavering commitment to personal growth.

It’s about recognizing that true success lies not solely in the destination but in the journey itself—the relentless pursuit of improvement, the determination to push boundaries, and the audacity to dream big. With a growth mindset, we step out of our comfort zones, embrace discomfort as a catalyst for growth, and unlock our boundless potential.

This mindset beckons us to be architects of our own destiny, where challenges become opportunities to learn, adapt, and thrive. It’s a mindset that celebrates progress over perfection, understanding that every step forward, no matter how small, is a triumph that propels us closer to our goals.

But the growth mindset is not just about personal growth—it’s about fostering a culture of empowerment, collaboration, and continuous improvement. It’s about supporting and lifting others as we rise, for we understand that when one person grows, we all do.
